extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, regulated parties, and agency staff seeking to understand or participate in federal notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide describing the federal informal rulemaking (notice-and-comment) process: what authorizes agencies, how rulemakings are started and announced, how proposed and final rules are structured, public participation options, timing rules, exceptions, codification, oversight, and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency statutory authority to issue regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies get their authority to issue regulations from laws (statutes) enacted by Congress; in some cases the President may delegate Presidential authority to an agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency must not take action that goes beyond its statutory authority or violates the Constitution. Agencies must follow an open public process when they issue regulations, according to the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). This includes publishing a statement of rulemaking authority in the Federal Register for all proposed and final rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors that may prompt agencies to begin rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies consider multiple factors in deciding to start rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: new technologies or new data; concerns from accidents or societal problems; recommendations from Congressional committees or federal advisory committees; petitions from interest groups/corporations/members of the public; lawsuits; Presidential directives; 'prompt letters' from OMB; requests from other agencies; studies and staff recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of Regulatory Plan and Unified Agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must publish a Regulatory Plan annually (fall) and an Agenda of Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions in spring and fall (Unified Agenda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Unified Agenda announces future rulemaking activities and updates the public on pending and completed regulatory actions. It is posted on RegInfo.gov and Regulations.gov and often in the Federal Register; collections are available on GPO FDsys/e-CFR resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public involvement before a proposed rule (preliminary outreach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may gather information through informal conversations, petitions for rulemaking, Advance Notices of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM), or negotiated rulemaking before publishing an NPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ANPRMs are formal invitations to participate and start the notice-and-comment process. Anyone (individuals and groups) may respond to ANPRMs to help develop or recommend against a rule. Negotiated rulemaking invites interested parties to meet and seek consensus that the agency may adopt as the proposed rule basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may participate in developing a proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone interested — individuals and groups — may submit input in pre-proposal steps and respond to ANPRMs and petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation can take the form of comments, petitions for rulemaking, attendance at negotiated rulemaking meetings, or responses to advance notices. Agencies may announce petitions in the Federal Register and accept public comments on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential/OIRA review of significant proposed rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The President, assisted by OIRA, may review draft proposed rules deemed 'significant' for economic effects or important policy issues prior to publication for public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For significant rules, the agency must estimate costs and benefits and consider alternative solutions. OIRA analyzes draft proposals; OIRA review is part of executive-branch oversight on significant regulatory actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) clearance for information collection
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed rule requires the public to provide information to the government, the agency must estimate the paperwork burden and obtain PRA approval from OIRA before proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must identify information collection burdens and secure necessary PRA clearance; related portions subject to later approval may be excepted from effective dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required impact analyses for significant rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may be required to analyze a proposed rule’s impact on small businesses; state, local, and tribal governments; families; federalism; just compensation; and unfunded mandates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These analyses are often part of executive orders or statutes and inform agency decisionmaking and OIRA review; agencies should consider these impacts and document them in the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and legal basis statement in the NPRM
rubrics_metrics.description: The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) must announce and explain the agency’s plan to address a problem or accomplish a goal and must be published in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All proposed rules must be published to notify the public and give opportunity to comment. The proposed rule and public comments form the basis of the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the proposed rule (preamble and regulatory text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed rules have preambles containing a Summary, Dates, Addresses, contact information, and Supplementary Information; followed by the regulatory text or a narrative description of proposed amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Summary' explains issues and necessity; 'Dates' and 'Addresses' state comment deadlines and submission methods; 'Supplementary Information' discusses merits, cites data, details choices and reasoning, and must identify legal authority. Agencies usually publish the regulatory text in full; if not, they must describe the action in narrative form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods and timing for public comment periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies generally specify comment periods (typically 30–60 days), but periods can be longer for complex rulemakings (e.g., 180+ days) or shorter when justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies set comment deadlines in the 'Dates' section of the Federal Register. Members of the public may request extensions; agencies may accept late-filed comments if schedule permits, but are generally not legally required to consider late submissions. Agencies indicate in proposed rules or procedural rules whether they will consider late comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons to re-open comments or issue multiple proposed rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may extend or re-open comment periods when they lack sufficient high-quality comments or when comments raise new issues; they may issue multiple proposed rules as new issues or complexity arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-opening or issuing supplemental proposals helps agencies gather more information or address issues raised. Substantive new issues may justify supplemental NPRMs; otherwise changes may be incorporated into the final rule if they are a logical outgrowth of the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional public participation options during comment period
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may gather comments via public hearings, rulemaking hearings (where required), public meetings, webcasts, and interactive internet sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the comment period, agencies may establish a reply comment period (optional) to allow responses to prior comments, fostering more public dialogue. Agencies use varied outreach methods to broaden participation and collect more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for electronic comments and their advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Most agencies prefer electronic comments because they are more easily available to the public and help agencies organize comments by subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic submission through agency docket sites or Regulations.gov improves accessibility and enables agencies to make more effective use of comments. Agencies often provide a button or instructions in Federal Register notices for submitting comments electronically.

rubrics_metrics.name: How public comments affect the final rule (record-based decisionmaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must base final rules on the rulemaking record — including comments, scientific data, expert opinions, and facts accumulated during pre-rule and proposed rule stages — not on vote counts of comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency cannot base a final rule on the number of comments for or against it. The agency must conclude that its proposed solution will help accomplish goals or solve problems and consider alternatives that might be more effective or less costly. Persuasive new data or arguments in the record may lead agencies to terminate, modify, or supplement the rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: When agencies must publish a supplemental proposed rule vs proceed to final
rubrics_metrics.description: If changes after comments are major or raise new issues not previously discussed, the agency should publish a supplemental proposed rule; minor changes or logical outgrowths may be adopted in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major changes triggered by new issues require another notice-and-comment cycle; minor or expected changes that follow from the original proposal may be finalized without a supplemental NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential/OIRA review of significant final rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The President and OIRA review draft final rules when they are 'significant' due to economic effects or important policy issues, prior to Federal Register publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA’s final analysis of estimated costs and benefits may consider comments and alternate solutions suggested in public comments. Interagency consultation may occur during this phase and is sometimes mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and required contents of the final rule preamble
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules have preambles with a Summary, Effective Date, and Supplementary Information; the agency must state the basis and purpose of the rule in the Supplementary Information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'basis and purpose' explains the goals/problems addressed, describes facts and data relied upon, responds to major criticisms from proposed-rule comments, and explains why alternatives were not chosen. The agency must identify legal authority and publish regulatory text in full, with instructions for amending the CFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard effective-date timing and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules are generally effective no less than 30 days after Federal Register publication; significant and major rules are required to have a 60-day delayed effective date, though exceptions exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency wants a sooner effective date, it must cite 'good cause' showing why the earlier effective date is in the public interest. Major rules defined under statute and Executive Order may require 60 days; emergency situations may allow earlier effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause and other exceptions to conventional notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA permits finalizing rules without a prior NPRM when there is 'good cause' that notice-and-comment would be impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical justifications: emergencies to avert threats to public health/safety, minor technical amendments/corrections with no substantive issues, or when Congress has directed a specific regulatory outcome. Agencies must state their reasoning for finding good cause in the preamble. Other exceptions allow straight-to-final for internal agency procedures, rules affecting only federal employees, and rules managing federal property, though these may still require proposed rulemaking if they affect the public substantially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim final rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency finds good cause to issue a final rule without prior NPRM, it may label it an 'interim final rule' that becomes effective immediately upon publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the agency states it will alter the interim rule if warranted by public comments; if no changes are made, the agency will publish a brief confirming finalization in the Federal Register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct final rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may publish a direct final rule when the changes are routine or uncontroversial, stating the rule will take effect on a date unless substantive adverse comments are received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adverse comments are submitted, the agency must withdraw the direct final rule before its effective date. The agency may then publish a conventional proposed rule or end the rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codification into the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) and e-CFR
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must publish CFR changes in the final rule with instructions for adding, revising, removing, or re-designating regulatory text; GPO/Office of the Federal Register process codifies rules into the CFR/e-CFR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On publication day, OFR and GPO begin processing material for e-CFR integration. Immediately effective rules are integrated into the e-CFR; delayed-effective rules are placed in amendment files and linked. The e-CFR is an unofficial but authoritative editorial compilation; official annual CFR editions are assembled from e-CFR material on a staggered quarterly basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional review and the Congressional Review Act (CRA)
rubrics_metrics.description: New final rules must be sent to Congress and GAO for review before they can take effect under the CRA; major rules must be effective at least 60 days after publication to allow Congressional review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress may pass a resolution of disapproval; if both houses pass and the President signs (or a veto is overridden), the rule is void and cannot be republished in the same form without Congressional approval. Congress also exercises oversight via hearings, legislation, or funding restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication activities: compliance, interpretation, and review
rubrics_metrics.description: After publication, the regulatory process continues with compliance assistance, interpretation, enforcement, guidance materials, and periodic review or amendment of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may publish guidance documents, compliance manuals, or interpretive rules to help the public understand requirements. Based on enforcement experience or changed conditions, agencies may amend, revoke, or let a rule stand; formal changes require notice-and-comment. Some statutes or directives may require formal reviews at set intervals or upon public petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive rules and policy statements vs legislative rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive rules and policy statements explain how an agency interprets existing regulations/statutes and help the public understand compliance, but must not set new legal standards or impose new requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance documents do not amend the CFR and are not subject to notice-and-comment, though agencies sometimes seek comments to improve clarity. Interpretive rules with broad applicability are often published in the Federal Register; others may appear only on agency websites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review of rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts can review rules to determine whether a rule is unconstitutional; exceeds the agency’s legal authority; was issued without required notice-and-comment; or was arbitrary, capricious, or an abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a court vacates all or part of a rule, it usually remands the rule to the agency to correct deficiencies. The agency may need to reopen the comment period, publish a new Statement of Basis and Purpose to justify decisions, or restart rulemaking by issuing a new proposed rule.
